title: They shared everything (Acts 2:37–47)
hookLine: the first community breaks bread in homes and shares what they own
tomorrow: the beggar at the Beautiful Gate

cards: A shared house has a group chat, and the group chat has opinions. Whose turn is it. Who ate the last of the bread.
Sharing sounds lovely until it's Tuesday. Back at Pentecost, the same day, Peter has just finished speaking, and Acts says the crowd were cut to the heart and asked: what shall we do?

He tells them to turn around and be baptized, and about three thousand people do, in a single day. Many are visitors far from home, and the small group from Galilee has no buildings, no budget and no plan.
What happens next, Luke tells in one short paragraph.

teach.b: Luke gives four things they kept doing: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer.
The word for fellowship is koinonia, from koinos, common, shared: having a share in something together.
Luke shows what that looked like: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and gave to anyone as they had need.

They met in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes, and here's the source of our line: they "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Meat, in the King James Bible's English, just means food.
Singleness of heart: a heart that isn't divided. Glad and simple hearts. Now the honest part.

Acts doesn't pretend it stayed easy. A few chapters later a couple lie about what they gave, and there's an argument about widows being left out of the daily food. Christians have read it in different ways ever since.
Monks and nuns took it as a pattern and hold everything in common to this day, as do some Protestant communities like the Hutterites.
Many other Christians read it as a picture of radical generosity, given freely, rather than a rule for every church. Whichever way you read it, nobody is told to share. They just do.
And the bread keeps turning up: in homes, around tables, day after day.

how: Many churches hold up Acts 2:42 as a pattern for church life: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Monastic communities and some Protestant communities hold property in common; many other Christians practice it through giving and shared meals.

o: the Greek name for a church building or hall
fellowship: having a share in something together
a vow to give up all your property for good

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the first Christians were ordered to give up their property
nobody is told to share. Acts describes them doing it, freely.
Acts admits the sharing ran into trouble
a couple lie about their gift, and there's an argument about widows left out of the food.
breaking of bread happened only in the temple
they met in the temple courts, and broke bread from house to house.

games.q: you're one of three thousand new believers in Jerusalem. some of them are far from home and have nothing. you own a field. what do you do?
o: keep it. the apostles will sort things out.
sell it and give to whoever has need.
wait and see what the others do.
games.why: Acts says they sold their possessions and goods and parted them to all, as every man had need, and ate with gladness.

practice: Let your mind walk through where you live, room by room: the shelf, the closet, the kitchen.

Look for one thing you have more of than you need, or something you love that someone else would love too, a book, a coat, a tool, a meal's worth of food, and without deciding how much, find one person or place it could go to.
If you pray, offer it to God first.

wordCard.voice: Koinonia. The Greek word for fellowship, a shared life, as the first believers lived it: breaking bread in homes and holding what they had in common.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, having a share in something together; from koinos, common.

carryVoice: Your line: glad and simple hearts. Tomorrow, a man at a gate asks for money and gets something else. Day seventy-six, complete.
